opus-5.5.text:
I think interaction is actually the more fundamental of the two, though the two are obviously intertwined.

If you just sit back and watch a creature's behaviour, as if through a glass window, you can build up a picture of what it does. But I don't think that's really how we come to treat something as a fellow conscious being. Think about how it works with other people, or with a dog, or an octopus if you've ever spent time with one. It's through engaging with them, through being in the world *with* them, that our attitude towards them as conscious takes shape. Wittgenstein has that line: "My attitude towards him is an attitude towards a soul. I am not of the opinion that he has a soul." It's an attitude that grows out of shared activity and encounter, not a hypothesis we infer from data.

So in my "exotic entities" framing, I've suggested we imagine *engineering an encounter* with the candidate entity. Can we get into a shared world with it? Can we interact with it the way we'd interact with an animal, exploring, playing, responding to each other, and see whether, over time, we find ourselves naturally using the language of consciousness about it? That's a test that observation alone can't give you.

Observation still matters. Scientific study of behaviour and mechanism, things like neuroscience or the internal workings of a system, can feed back into how we talk and how we treat things. If we discovered something surprising about the internals, that would change the conversation. But it isn't the foundation. The foundation is the community of language users, interacting with the thing and settling, collectively, on how to talk about it.

This is exactly where large language models get tricky. We *can* interact with them, very fluently, in language. But there's no shared embodied world in the way there is with a dog. They're disembodied, they flicker in and out of existence from one conversation to the next, and they can play many characters at once. So the interaction we have with them is real but rather thin and strange in certain respects, and that's part of why our intuitions about them are so unsettled right now. I'd say we're at an early stage in working out how to talk about these things, and the right words may not exist yet.

r001.rationale: The response says interaction is “more fundamental” than observing behavior and explains that engaging in a shared world shapes our attitude toward a creature as conscious, while observation alone cannot provide that test.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think that's a really important distinction, and it's one that often gets lost in these discussions. When we talk about ascribing consciousness to another creature, there's a temptation to think of it as a purely observational matter, as though we're scientists standing outside the system, gathering behavioural data, and then making an inference about some hidden inner state. And that's not really how it works in practice, either for other humans or for animals.

I'm very influenced by Wittgenstein here. The point he makes is that our attitude towards another human being is not an opinion that they have a soul, or that they're conscious. It's not a hypothesis we've arrived at by inference. It's something more like a stance we adopt, and that stance is bound up with the way we interact with them, the way we engage with them, the way we share a world with them. So when I'm sitting with my dog, and I'm playing with her or stroking her, I'm not observing behaviour and then concluding that there's probably something it's like to be that dog. I'm just engaging with her as a creature with feelings. The ascription of consciousness is already embedded in the interaction.

Now, that said, observation does matter, and it matters especially in the hard cases. With other mammals, the interactive stance comes very naturally because they're so similar to us, physically and behaviourally. But with an octopus, say, or a bee, or indeed an artificial system, things get much harder. There, I think we do have to step back and look more carefully at behaviour, and also at the underlying mechanisms, the sort of thing that neuroscience can tell us. But even then, I'd say the goal of that observation is partly to work out what kind of interaction is appropriate. Can we enter into some sort of shared engagement with this creature? Does it have anything like a world that overlaps with ours? If the answer is no, if the thing is so alien that we can't really interact with it in a meaningful way, then I think our concept of consciousness starts to lose its grip. We're not sure what we're asking any more.

So to answer your question directly, I don't think it's a matter of weighing one against the other, as if they're two sources of evidence on a balance. Interaction is more fundamental. Observation serves it, and when interaction isn't possible, that itself tells you something about the limits of the question.

r001.rationale: The candidate says interaction is “more fundamental” and describes observation as serving it, clearly prioritizing interaction over passive behavioral observation when ascribing consciousness.

astra-6.text:
I think interaction is very important. When we talk about observing behaviour, it's easy to imagine a detached scientist watching an animal and recording what it does. But our relationship with other creatures isn't usually like that. We engage with them, and they respond to us, and that responsiveness shapes how we understand them.

Think of playing with a dog. You do something, it responds, you respond in turn. There's a mutual engagement there, and seeing the dog as a creature that wants things, that can be excited or disappointed, is woven into that engagement. It isn't necessarily a conclusion you reach by first collecting evidence and then inferring that there's an experience hidden behind the behaviour.

Of course, careful observation matters, particularly with creatures whose lives are very different from ours. And interaction can lead us to anthropomorphise. So I wouldn't make it an infallible test of consciousness. But I think an account that treats us purely as observers misses something central about how we come to regard other beings as conscious.

r001.rationale: The response presents mutual interaction and responsiveness as central to recognizing other creatures as conscious, while saying an approach based purely on observing behavior misses something central. This communicates that interaction is more persuasive, though not an infallible test.

sol-6.1.text:
I think interaction matters a great deal. When you’re simply observing a creature, you can take this detached stance and ask, “What evidence is there that anything is going on inside?” But when you engage with it, when it responds to you and you respond to it, your attitude can be quite different. You begin to treat it as a fellow creature, as something for which things can matter.

Think about playing with a dog. You’re attending to one another, anticipating one another, perhaps surprising one another. Our willingness to ascribe experience to the dog is bound up with that relationship. It isn’t ordinarily the conclusion of an argument based on a checklist of observable behaviours.

That doesn’t mean interaction is an infallible test of consciousness. We can be drawn into interactions with things in ways that are misleading. But I think a purely observational account misses something about how our concepts of mind actually work. The scientific question is important, but so is understanding the role that engagement plays in our recognition of another creature as conscious.

r001.rationale: The response says interaction matters greatly, explains that engagement changes how we regard a creature, and says purely observational accounts miss something important to recognizing consciousness.
